headline: Orient Point rips fire as bunker schools push through Plum Gut
subhead: Bass to 35 pounds crash bait pods while porgy action heats up the oyster cages.
body_markdown:
Sixty years walking these beaches, and I still get that tingle when the water starts talking. This week, she's been downright chatty.

The big news is Orient Point. Tuesday morning, just after slack water turned to flood, I watched the most beautiful thing — acres of bunker getting pushed through Plum Gut like someone was herding cattle. Bass were underneath them, rolling and slashing, some real cows in the mix. Tommy Kowalski put his nephew on a 35-pounder that morning, fish took a live bunker on a circle hook right in the white water where the rip meets the point. Kid fought it for twenty minutes before Tommy could get the net under her.

The key is timing the tide change. You want to be set up on the west side of the point as the flood starts pushing. Those bunker schools get compressed against the rocks, and the bass know it. I've been running 6-inch live bunker on fishfinder rigs, 6/0 circles, 30-pound leader. Let the current do the work — no need to get fancy when the fish are that aggressive.

Further west along my beat, the oyster cages off Rocky Point have been holding decent porgy. Nothing huge — mostly 12 to 14 inches — but steady picking if you can deal with the current. Green crabs on high-low rigs, size 4 hooks. The trick is anchoring uptide of the cages and letting your rig swing down into the structure. Water's been running clean, maybe 8 to 10 feet of visibility, which has the porgy feeding confident.

Horton Point's been giving up some nice bluefish in the evenings. Cocktail blues mostly, 3 to 5 pounds, but they're thick when the tide's moving. Kastmasters and Deadly Dicks work fine, but I've had better luck with small poppers right at sunset. Something about that surface commotion when the light's fading — gets them fired up.

Water temperature's been climbing steady. Hit 64 degrees at Orient Point yesterday, which is right where it should be for mid-June. That's warm enough to pull the weakfish up from deeper water, and I'm starting to see signs. Found some small pods of grass shrimp in the shallows off Mattituck Inlet Tuesday evening, which usually means the weaks aren't far behind. Haven't connected yet, but I'm watching.

The bait situation tells the whole story. Besides those bunker schools moving through the Gut, I'm seeing good numbers of spearing along the rocky shoreline and sand eels in the deeper pockets. The spearing are what's keeping the smaller bass around — 20 to 28 inch fish that are perfect for the table. Small Clouser Minnows on light spinning gear, or just a size 2 hook with a piece of spearing if you want to keep it simple.

Moon's waxing toward full this weekend, which should push more bait through the system. Spring tides always stir things up, especially in Plum Gut where the current can really rip. I'm planning to be at Orient Point Saturday morning, early flood tide, with a cooler full of fresh bunker. If this pattern holds, it could be the start of something special.

One thing I've learned in six decades out here — when the water's this clean and the bait's moving like this, you don't overthink it. Keep your tackle simple, watch the tide, and let the fish tell you what they want. Right now, they're saying bunker and they're saying Orient Point. I'd listen if I were you.
